displayQuote: Brevity is the soul of wit

meta.title: Who really said "Brevity is the soul of wit"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Really Shakespeare — Polonius says it in Hamlet 2.2, printed in the 1604 quarto. But “wit” meant wisdom, and the speaker is the play’s windbag.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Brevity is the soul of wit'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified to Hamlet, Act 2, Scene 2, spoken by Polonius. Confirmed in the 1604 quarto and the 1623 First Folio — and the joke is on the speaker.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuine Shakespeare, and locatable to the line: it is spoken by Polonius in Hamlet, Act 2, Scene 2, and stands in the 1604 quarto as well as the 1623 First Folio. The catch is that Shakespeare wrote it as a self-satirising line for the play’s biggest windbag, and that “wit” then meant wisdom, not humour.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Polonius, reporting to Claudius and Gertrude on the prince’s madness
The 1604 quarto (the Folger’s copy); the First Folio of 1623, at TLN 1117
“Therefore, since Breuitie is the Soule of Wit,”

source.excerpt:
My liege, and madam, to expostulate
What majesty should be, what duty is,
Why day is day, night night, and time is time
Were nothing but to waste night, day, and time.
Therefore, since brevity is the soul of wit,
And tediousness the limbs and outward flourishes,
I will be brief. Your noble son is mad.
trail: The Folger Shakespeare Library’s text of Hamlet 2.2 ↗ carries the line inside Polonius’s speech to the king and queen, immediately before “Your noble son is mad.”

Internet Shakespeare Editions’ old-spelling First Folio text ↗ prints it at TLN 1117 as “Therefore, since Breuitie is the Soule of Wit,” followed by “And tediousnesse, the limbes and outward flourishes,”.

Quote Investigator ↗, investigating Dorothy Parker’s riff on it, reproduces the 1604 quarto held by the Folger — “Therefore breuitie is the soule of wit, And tediousnes the lymmes and outward florishes” — and explains that “wit” then meant wisdom.
Wikiquote’s Hamlet page ↗ lists the full sentence under Polonius, Act II, scene ii, with no dispute noted.
source.excerptNote: Four lines of pure padding, and then a boast about not padding. Polonius keeps going after this for some time before he reaches anything resembling a point.

source.rightsNote: Hamlet was in print in Shakespeare’s lifetime — the Folger dates the “good quarto” to 1604 in some copies and 1605 in others, and the play was collected in the First Folio of 1623. Any work published that long before 1931 is in the public domain in the United States, so the text of the line carries no copyright; only a modern editor’s apparatus, notes or glosses in a particular edition could.

author.name: William Shakespeare
author.heading: About William Shakespeare
author.bio: Shakespeare was baptised at Stratford-upon-Avon on 26 April 1564 and died on 23 April 1616; the traditional birth date of 23 April 1564 is given even though the exact day is unknown. He worked as an actor and house dramatist in London, and is widely regarded as the greatest writer in the English language. Hamlet is the source of an unusual number of lines that escaped the play and became proverbs on their own — this is one of them, and like several others it was written to be faintly ridiculous in its original mouth.

misattribution.heading: What gets garbled
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right, which is unusual for a line this famous. What travels wrongly is who says it, what it meant, and where it stops.

items.why: Shakespeare wrote it, but he gave it to Polonius as self-satire. myShakespeare’s note on the line is blunt about the effect: “The irony here is of course that Polonius is being anything but brief” ↗. Quoting it as the author’s sincere maxim throws away the point.

items.who: the modern sense of “wit” as humour
items.why: Quote Investigator notes that “in the Bard’s time the word ‘wit’ had a different sense, and the adage meant roughly: the essence of wisdom is being concise” ↗. Read as advice about comedy, it is a different sentence from the one Shakespeare wrote.

In the play the clause is subordinate and paired with its opposite: “Therefore, since brevity is the soul of wit, / And tediousness the limbs and outward flourishes, / I will be brief. Your noble son is mad.” ↗ The aphorism as usually quoted drops both the “since” and the tediousness half of the figure.

Parker’s line is the parody, not the original. Quote Investigator concludes that “Dorothy Parker should be credited with the expression ‘Brevity is the soul of lingerie’” ↗, in a caption she wrote for Vogue in October 1916, reusing it in Vanity Fair in May 1919.

misattribution.truthLine: The six words are Shakespeare’s, written for Polonius in Hamlet 2.2 and in print by 1604 — the 1623 Folio sets them at TLN 1117 ↗. They just were never meant to be taken at face value.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: Polonius has been sent to explain what is wrong with the prince, and instead of explaining it he circles the subject — majesty, duty, why day is day and night night — before announcing that he will not waste anyone’s time. The maxim is the hinge of a joke: he praises brevity in the middle of the most tediously padded speech he has yet delivered, and myShakespeare puts it plainly — “The irony here is of course that Polonius is being anything but brief” ↗.

The line then walked out of the play and lost the joke. Quoted alone it reads as straightforward writing advice, which is roughly the opposite of its dramatic function, and it acquired a second meaning along the way: Quote Investigator notes that in Shakespeare’s time “wit” meant wisdom, so the adage meant that the essence of wisdom is being concise ↗ — not that short jokes are funnier.
context.detailsSummary: The 1604 quarto and the 1623 Folio do not read identically
detailsBody: The version most people recite — “Therefore, since brevity is the soul of wit” — matches the First Folio, where Internet Shakespeare Editions prints “Therefore, since Breuitie is the Soule of Wit,” at TLN 1117 ↗. Quote Investigator, reproducing the 1604 quarto held by the Folger, gives it without the “since”: “Therefore breuitie is the soule of wit, And tediousnes the lymmes and outward florishes, I will be briefe, your noble sonne is mad” ↗. Either way the six famous words are identical; only the conjunction moves.

That difference is ordinary for this play. The Folger explains that Hamlet survives in three early printings — a 1603 quarto it calls “generally unreliable as a witness to what was written for the stage” ↗, the “good quarto” dated 1604 in some copies and 1605 in others, and the 1623 Folio — and that modern editions, its own included, blend the second quarto with as much of the Folio as they can.
context.pull: A windbag’s excuse for not being a windbag, now quoted as if it were a rule.
